sections.title: The NATO phonetic alphabet is the standard method used on ma
sections.text:
The NATO phonetic alphabet is the standard method used on marine VHF radio to spell out letters, call signs, vessel names, and place names without ambiguity. Static, weak signal strength, and similar-sounding letters (such as "B" and "D", or "M" and "N") make plain letter-by-letter spelling unreliable over radio. The International Telecommunication Union (ITU) Radio Regulations, and in turn the IMO and national maritime authorities, require operators to use this standardized alphabet whenever spelling is necessary, for example when giving a vessel name, a call sign, a position name, or a person's surname during a distress, urgency, or routine call.

The Standard Alphabet Table

Each letter of the English alphabet has one single, standardized code word, and every trained VHF operator must know all twenty-six by heart. The letter A is spoken as Alpha. The letter B is spoken as Bravo. The letter C is spoken as Charlie. The letter D is spoken as Delta. The letter E is spoken as Echo. The letter F is spoken as Foxtrot. The letter G is spoken as Golf. The letter H is spoken as Hotel. The letter I is spoken as India. The letter J is spoken as Juliett.

The letter K is spoken as Kilo. The letter L is spoken as Lima. The letter M is spoken as Mike. The letter N is spoken as November. The letter O is spoken as Oscar. The letter P is spoken as Papa. The letter Q is spoken as Quebec. The letter R is spoken as Romeo. The letter S is spoken as Sierra. The letter T is spoken as Tango.

The letter U is spoken as Uniform. The letter V is spoken as Victor. The letter W is spoken as Whiskey. The letter X is spoken as X-ray. The letter Y is spoken as Yankee. The letter Z is spoken as Zulu.

sections.title: Pronunciation of Numbers
sections.text:
Numbers are also given their own standardized pronunciation on VHF radio to avoid confusion, particularly between numbers that sound alike when spoken quickly. Zero is pronounced ZERO. One is pronounced WUN. Two is pronounced TOO. Three is pronounced TREE. Four is pronounced FOWER. Five is pronounced FIFE. Six is pronounced SIX. Seven is pronounced SEVEN. Eight is pronounced AIT. Nine is pronounced NINER. Each digit of a multi-digit number, such as a call sign or a position, is read out individually rather than as a whole number, for example the number 79 is transmitted as SEVEN NINER, not as seventy-nine.

Why the Phonetic Alphabet Matters

Using the correct phonetic alphabet is not optional politeness, it is a regulatory requirement under the ITU Radio Regulations because misheard letters in a vessel name, call sign, or position can delay a search and rescue response or cause a message to be logged incorrectly by a coast station or Vessel Traffic Service. Before transmitting a spelled-out word, the operator should say "I SPELL" so the listening station knows individual letters are about to follow rather than a normal word, and should read the word back once at normal pace afterward so the listener can confirm they understood correctly.
